summary: Sets out the Internet best current practice for assigning entries under URI.ARPA, the domain used by the DDDS system for URI resolution. It is part five of the DDDS series. It was later updated by RFC 8958.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 3405 sets rules for adding DNS records that help resolve URI schemes and URN namespaces. Registration follows a public review process, and the rules must be tied to an already registered scheme or namespace.

subtitle: The review and registration process for DNS-based URI and URN resolution rules.

tldr.problem: DNS-based URI resolution needs a controlled way to add rules to URI.ARPA and URN.ARPA without allowing unsafe delegation changes.
tldr.mechanism: A URI scheme or URN namespace must be registered first. A request gives the key, responsible authority, and NAPTR records, then goes to an open list for a two-week objection period before IANA enters it.
tldr.outcome: RFC 3405 is a Best Current Practice updated by RFC 8958. It recommends keeping changeable resolution details outside the long-lived arpa zones.

today: RFC 3405 is a Best Current Practice and is updated by RFC 8958. It is not marked as obsoleted in the unit metadata.

sections.title: What URI.ARPA and URN.ARPA Do
sections.content:
RFC 3405 is part five of the Dynamic Delegation Discovery System series. It describes how to add Naming Authority Pointer (NAPTR) records to URI.ARPA and URN.ARPA for DNS-based resolution.

A URI lookup starts by appending URI.ARPA to its scheme; for example, the RFC uses http.URI.ARPA. URN resolution begins with a rule in URI.ARPA and then looks up a namespace identifier under URN.ARPA.
sections.plainLanguage: A DNS lookup can use URI.ARPA to find the first rule for a URI scheme. URNs use that first rule to find a second rule under URN.ARPA.

sections.title: Registration Comes Before DNS Rules
sections.content:
A URI scheme must first be registered under the IETF URI tree, with a stable published specification. A URN namespace identifier must also be registered before its NAPTR record can be added.

The IESG or a designated expert reviews the request for correctness, consistency with the published specification, and possible delegation risks. If an outside party controls the specification, the owner or maintainer must approve the DNS registration.
sections.plainLanguage: First register and document the URI scheme or URN namespace. Only then can its DNS rule be reviewed for addition.

sections.title: Keep Changeable Rules Outside arpa
sections.content:
The URI.ARPA and URN.ARPA records are expected to have very long time-to-live values. If a resolution rule is likely to change, the stable arpa record should point to a record in a less stable DNS zone.

The RFC contrasts a flexible URN namespace, whose detailed rules belong elsewhere, with the HTTP scheme, whose host information follows a fixed syntax and can be handled by a stable URI.ARPA rule.
sections.plainLanguage: Records in arpa are expected to remain unchanged for a long time. If a rule changes often, the arpa entry should point to a separate place that can be updated more often.

sections.title: Submitting and Reviewing a Request
sections.content:
A request is sent to an open mailing list: register@URI.ARPA for URI schemes or register@URN.ARPA for URN namespaces. If no DNS-related objection is raised within two weeks, a representative of IANA considers the request accepted and enters it in the name server.

The template contains the key, the authority responsible for registration, and the DNS records. Objections must concern the arpa zone or DNS generally; objections to the scheme or namespace belong in their own registration process.
sections.plainLanguage: The requester sends a form to a public mailing list. If no one raises a DNS-related objection within two weeks, IANA enters the record.

sections.title: Security and IANA Considerations
sections.content:
IANA manages the URI.ARPA and URN.ARPA zones and the associated discussion lists. Their records are subject to the review process in this RFC.

The RFC identifies denial of service and forged records that redirect delegation paths as threats. Operators of the zones should secure them as Internet infrastructure and should sign records when they can do so reliably.
sections.plainLanguage: These zones are important targets because forged records could redirect lookups. The RFC says their operators should protect the zones and sign records when reliable signing is available.
